**I lean YES.** The likeliest qualifying event is UTJ and Yashar formally opening talks on Sunday, November 29, with rabbinic approval. An approval given on Thursday, November 26, would not itself count. ([timesofisrael.com](https://www.timesofisrael.com/liveblog_entry/utj-rabbis-said-to-give-go-ahead-to-launching-official-talks-with-eisenkot/))

**Base rate.** I’d start below even odds for UTJ to make a cross-bloc move official in any specified two-day window. The 2021 Bennett–Lapid coalition left UTJ in Netanyahu’s bloc, while the 2020 precedent brought UTJ into a government that included both Netanyahu and Gantz. Those are useful political comparisons, not enough cases to estimate a reliable two-day base rate. ([timesofisrael.com](https://www.timesofisrael.com/netanyahu-and-gantz-trade-barbs-rule-out-any-future-coalition-together/?utm_source=openai))

**What moves this case.** On November 24, Ynet reported that UTJ was assembling a formal negotiating team (**up**). On November 26, The Times of Israel reported that the rabbis had already given the go-ahead, while N12 quoted Hirsch’s office saying approval had not yet been given. Neither account establishes an in-window decision, but both point to the process being close to one (**up**). The most important distinction is that N12 and Channel 13 reported a first *bilateral* meeting on Sunday, whereas The Times of Israel described Sunday morning’s meeting as *internal* preparation with UTJ’s lawyer. The bilateral meeting is the strongest reason to lean YES; the internal meeting alone would not qualify. On November 27, Bennett signaled openness to an alternative if unity talks failed (**up**), but his preference for a Likud deal and the unresolved draft dispute still make a short delay plausible (**down**). ([ynet.co.il](https://www.ynet.co.il/news/article/bjzcphxkml?utm_source=openai))

### 3. Strongest Reason the Obvious Outcome Might Fail
While all preparations point toward Sunday as the decision and launch day—with an agreement in principle on draft exemptions already reached, a Sunday morning strategy meeting with counsel scheduled, and Eisenkot aiming to submit coalition deals by December 1–2—there are three significant ways the YES criterion could fail within the 48-hour window:

2. **Drafting / Intra-Bloc Friction on Sunday:** UTJ's lawmakers are meeting attorney Boaz Ben Tzur on Sunday morning to review the draft legislation framework before opening formal talks. If legal hurdles regarding Supreme Court scrutiny or pushback from Bennett's B'Yachad stall the morning review, formal authorisation or the official opening of talks could easily slip past 23:59 on Sunday into Monday.
3. **Media Reporting Threshold:** Because Kan, Ynet, and *The Times of Israel* already framed Thursday evening's meeting between Lando and Hirsch as giving the "green light" (which the criterion excludes as 26–27 November reporting), if Sunday features only internal legal consultations by UTJ without a formal opening session with Yashar or a newly reported rabbinic decree on Sunday, at least two of the specified outlets might not report a *new* authorisation or formal opening occurring inside the weekend window.

runs.reason:
The base rate for a reported, conditional Haredi rabbinic green light actually landing inside a two-day window is modest. In this negotiation cycle, outlets have repeatedly described UTJ as on the verge of formal talks, only for the Degel HaTorah leadership to withhold a clear authorization. When a rival track (here a possible Likud rotation) is still open, such decisions more often slip or are deferred than they are issued on the media’s timetable. A fair base rate for YES under this narrow criterion is about 0.45.

Dated reporting moves the case only somewhat above that. As of Friday 27 November, Maariv via the Jerusalem Post stated that formal authorization had not yet been granted, that the rabbis were inclined to allow formal Yashar talks if Netanyahu did not accept a rotation by Saturday night, and that final approval was not expected before Sunday, which the same account called the turning point. That is the main upward pull, reinforced by the December 6 mandate deadline and the bloc’s aim to sign agreements around 1–2 December. Pulling the other way, the same Friday reporting said Rabbi Hirsch still had to be briefed by MKs before deciding, and that real gaps remained on sanctions, arrests, and yeshiva funding. Israel National News reported the same day that Thursday’s Lando–Hirsch meeting barely touched politics, undercutting the premature Thursday-night “go-ahead” stories the criterion already excludes. Separately, the Jerusalem Post reported that Netanyahu was considering a weekend announcement that he would serve second in a rotation.

The obvious YES path is therefore a Sunday authorization after no credible Netanyahu move. That can fail if he does announce, or if the rabbis simply tell the MKs to wait for clarity on a Likud–Yashar deal, or if the Sunday briefing produces another deferral past 23:59. Any of those is NO under the criterion as written.
